06_weight_decay.svg: Computed, after Bishop (2006), Figure 1.7. Four panels left to right: no penalty, lambda equals 10 to the minus 7, 10 to the minus 3, and 1. Each plots y (vertical, minus 1 to 1) against x (horizontal, 0 to 1): a dashed sine-shaped curve the points were drawn from, ten magenta training points, 25 open green circles for new points, and the blue fitted degree-9 polynomial. Under each panel: training RMSE 0.00, 0.12, 0.18, 0.49; test RMSE 0.86, 0.34, 0.34, 0.61; length of the weight vector 1.1 million, 190, 17, 0.65. Without a penalty the curve passes through every training point and swings far off between them; with a small penalty it follows the dashed curve; with lambda equals 1 it is almost flat. The point: the penalty keeps the weights small and the curve smooth, and too large a penalty underfits.
06_weight_decay_coef0.svg: The same four panels as the weight-penalty figure, with the first panel, no penalty, drawn in full and the other three dimmed. Its ten fitted coefficients are written out below: y equals minus 0.12, minus 160 x, plus 3.9 thousand x squared, minus 35 thousand x cubed, plus 160 thousand x to the fourth, minus 430 thousand x to the fifth, plus 680 thousand x to the sixth, minus 650 thousand x to the seventh, plus 340 thousand x to the eighth, minus 75 thousand x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.00, test RMSE 0.86, length of the weight vector 1.1 million. The point: huge coefficients of alternating sign are what let the curve swing between the ten points.
06_weight_decay_coef1.svg: The same four panels, with the second panel, lambda equals 10 to the minus 7, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals minus 0.13, plus 13 x, minus 46 x squared, plus 46 x cubed, plus 31 x to the fourth, minus 82 x to the fifth, minus 37 x to the sixth, plus 76 x to the seventh, plus 91 x to the eighth, minus 91 x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.12, test RMSE 0.34, length of the weight vector 190. The point: a tiny penalty already brings every coefficient under 100 and the curve close to the dashed one.
06_weight_decay_coef2.svg: The same four panels, with the third panel, lambda equals 10 to the minus 3, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals 0.10, plus 6.1 x, minus 12 x squared, minus 4.0 x cubed, plus 2.7 x to the fourth, plus 5.4 x to the fifth, plus 5.1 x to the sixth, plus 2.6 x to the seventh, minus 1.0 x to the eighth, minus 5.4 x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.18, test RMSE 0.34, length of the weight vector 17. The point: every coefficient is under 12, the curve is smooth, and the error on new points is as low as with the smaller penalty.
06_weight_decay_coef3.svg: The same four panels, with the fourth panel, lambda equals 1, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals 0.35, minus 0.27 x, minus 0.34 x squared, minus 0.25 x cubed, minus 0.14 x to the fourth, minus 0.059 x to the fifth, plus 0.0053 x to the sixth, plus 0.053 x to the seventh, plus 0.088 x to the eighth, plus 0.11 x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.49, test RMSE 0.61, length of the weight vector 0.65. The point: every coefficient is under 0.35, the fitted curve is nearly a flat line, and the error rises on training and new points alike: too large a penalty underfits.
encoding_fit_heldout.svg: Computed: one monkey IT recording site (Bao et al., 2020) predicted from 512 units of an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18's late layer by ridge regression, a random fifth of the 1,224 images held out. Left panel: predicted response (vertical, 0 to 60) against recorded response (horizontal, 0 to about 75), with a dashed diagonal where the two are equal; faint magenta dots are training images, larger green dots held-out images, both spread along the diagonal. Labels: held-out R squared 0.69, training R squared 0.71. Right panel: R squared (vertical, 0 to 1) against the penalty lambda on a log axis from 10 to the minus 2 to 10 to the 5. With almost no penalty the magenta training curve is at 0.85 and the green held-out curve at 0.28; as the penalty grows they meet near 0.69 at a dotted vertical line, the lambda chosen by cross-validation within the training images, then both fall. The point: too small a penalty overfits, and the penalty is chosen without the held-out images.
dropout.svg: Schematic: three copies of the same small network, an input layer of four units, two hidden layers of five, and two output units, drawn as light blue circles joined by grey lines. Left, training step 1: five of the ten hidden units are crossed out and have no connections, one in the first hidden layer and four in the second. Middle, training step 2: a different five are crossed out, two in the first hidden layer and three in the second. Right, test: all units are on and every connection is drawn; caption, outputs scaled to match training, hidden units times 0.5. The point: at each training step a random half of the hidden units is switched off, so no unit can rely on a particular partner; at test time all are on.
02_poly_samples.svg: Computed, after Bishop (2006), Figure 1.6. Four panels left to right: the same degree-9 polynomial fitted to N equals 10, 15, 30 and 100 points. Each panel plots y (vertical, minus 1 to 1) against x (horizontal, 0 to 1): a dashed sine-shaped curve, magenta training points, 25 open green circles for new points, and the blue fitted curve. Under each panel: training RMSE 0.00, 0.21, 0.21, 0.28; test RMSE 0.86, 0.34, 0.35, 0.31; the length of the weight vector 1.1 million, 46 thousand, 37 thousand, 8.7 thousand. With 10 points the curve swings far off between them; with 100 it follows the dashed curve through the noise. The point: the same model, with no penalty, overfits less as the number of examples grows.
02_poly_samples_coef0.svg: The same four panels as the more-examples figure, with the first panel, N equals 10 points, drawn in full and the other three dimmed. Its ten fitted coefficients are written out below and are the same as the unpenalized fit: y equals minus 0.12, minus 160 x, plus 3.9 thousand x squared, minus 35 thousand x cubed, plus 160 thousand x to the fourth, minus 430 thousand x to the fifth, plus 680 thousand x to the sixth, minus 650 thousand x to the seventh, plus 340 thousand x to the eighth, minus 75 thousand x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.00, test RMSE 0.86, length of the weight vector 1.1 million.
02_poly_samples_coef1.svg: The same four panels, with the second panel, N equals 15 points, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals minus 0.44, plus 16 x, minus 170 x squared, plus 1.6 thousand x cubed, minus 8.0 thousand x to the fourth, plus 21 thousand x to the fifth, minus 31 thousand x to the sixth, plus 25 thousand x to the seventh, minus 10 thousand x to the eighth, plus 1.6 thousand x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.21, test RMSE 0.34, length of the weight vector 46 thousand. The point: five more points cut the weights by a factor of about 20 and the error on new points by more than half.
02_poly_samples_coef2.svg: The same four panels, with the third panel, N equals 30 points, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals 0.52, minus 14 x, plus 220 x squared, minus 760 x cubed, minus 450 x to the fourth, plus 8.4 thousand x to the fifth, minus 21 thousand x to the sixth, plus 25 thousand x to the seventh, minus 15 thousand x to the eighth, plus 3.4 thousand x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.21, test RMSE 0.35, length of the weight vector 37 thousand. The point: the coefficients are still in the tens of thousands, but the curve stays close to the dashed one.
02_poly_samples_coef3.svg: The same four panels, with the fourth panel, N equals 100 points, drawn in full and the others dimmed. Its fitted coefficients, written out below: y equals minus 0.24, plus 25 x, minus 260 x squared, plus 1.3 thousand x cubed, minus 3.4 thousand x to the fourth, plus 3.8 thousand x to the fifth, plus 450 x to the sixth, minus 5.1 thousand x to the seventh, plus 4.5 thousand x to the eighth, minus 1.3 thousand x to the ninth. Under the panel: training RMSE 0.28, test RMSE 0.31, length of the weight vector 8.7 thousand. The point: with 100 points the curve can no longer swing between them; the training error rises toward the noise level of 0.30 and the error on new points is the lowest of the four.
07_augmentation.png: Computed with torchvision on one THINGSplus photograph of a pink orchid in front of dark green leaves. Eight square versions in two rows of four, each labelled above. Top row: Original; Horizontal flip, the mirror image; Resized crop, a zoomed-in part of the flower filling the square; Colour jitter, the same view with shifted colour and brightness. Bottom row: Rotation, the photo turned by a few tens of degrees with black corners; Affine warp, sheared and shifted with black wedges at the edges; Perspective, the photo squeezed as if seen at an angle inside a black frame; Random erasing, the original with a grey rectangle covering part of the flower. The point: every version still shows an orchid, so each can be a new training example with the same label.
mlp_vs_cnn.svg: Schematic: two panels over the same 6 by 6 grey-level image, a grid of grey squares at the bottom of each. Left, dense (multilayer perceptron): six hidden units above the image, each joined to all 36 pixels by thin grey lines, a tangle of 216 lines, and four output units joined to all six hidden units; caption, every pixel to every unit, 36 times 6 weights in the first layer, all different. Right, convolutional: a 4 by 4 map of hidden units; three are drawn wired each to its own 3 by 3 patch of pixels, the nine lines in the same nine colours for every unit; above, a 3 by 3 second-layer map with one unit wired to a 2 by 2 patch of the first map; caption, each unit sees a 3 by 3 patch, the 9 weights are shared by all 16 units. The point: a convolutional layer wires each unit to a local patch and reuses the same weights at every position.
param_count.svg: Computed: two horizontal bars on a log axis labelled weights in the first layer (log scale), from 10 to the 3 to 10 to the 8. Top bar, magenta: 96 filters of 11 by 11 by 3, reused at every position, 34,848 weights. Bottom bar, slate grey and much longer: 96 dense units, each wired to every pixel of a 224 by 224 colour image, 14,450,688 weights. The point: on a log axis the dense layer's bar runs almost three decades further, about 400 times more weights for the same 96 units.
conv_frame1.png: Computed. Three items left to right joined by arrows. The tiger photograph in grey levels, labelled image 224 by 224. An 11 by 11 Gabor filter, labelled filter 11 by 11: a small grid of grey squares with a bright stripe between two dark stripes, tilted about 20 degrees from vertical. The feature map, labelled feature map 224 by 224: a dark square with bright magenta and orange streaks wherever the tiger has stripes at the filter's orientation, mostly on the body and legs. The point: one set of weights is applied at every position, and the map keeps the image's layout, so shifting the image shifts the map.
conv_frame2.png: Computed: the same tiger photograph, labelled image 224 by 224 by 1, an arrow to four 11 by 11 Gabor filters at four orientations stacked as offset cards, labelled 4 filters, 11 by 11, and an arrow to four feature maps stacked as offset cards in the same dark-to-orange colour map as the single map before, labelled 4 feature maps: 224 by 224 by 4. The front map shows the near-vertical stripes; the maps behind it respond to the other three orientations. The point: each filter gives one map, so the layer's output is a stack with one channel per filter, and that stack is the next layer's input.
s12_img00_noletters.png: DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust (2012), Figure 1. Left: a side view of the macaque brain with the ventral visual stream coloured, V1 in red at the back, V2 green, V4 blue, and the inferior temporal cortex in yellow divided into PIT, CIT and AIT toward the front; below, an eye, an arrow to a box labelled LGN, and an arrow from the LGN to V1. Right: the same areas stacked as boxes from bottom to top with the typical response latency beside each: LGN about 40 milliseconds, V1 about 50, V2 about 60, V4 about 70, PIT about 80, CIT about 90, AIT about 100. Each box carries an approximate neuron count, from about 190 million in V1 to about 16 million in AIT, and arrows between stages give the size of each representation, from about 1 million at the LGN to about 10 million at IT. The point: the ventral stream is a hierarchy of areas, each adding about 10 milliseconds.
portrait_kuffler.png: A black-and-white head-and-shoulders photograph of Stephen W. Kuffler, the physiologist who mapped the centre-surround receptive fields of retinal ganglion cells in 1953. An older man with a high forehead and receding hair, smiling broadly, in a light open-collared shirt, looking slightly to the left of the camera. His name is printed under the photograph. The portrait sits in the top-right corner of the slide, above the caption Stephen Kuffler.
rf_icons_lgn.svg: Schematic: two circular receptive fields side by side. Left, an on-centre cell: a pink inner disc marked with three magenta plus signs, inside a light blue ring marked with four blue minus signs. Right, an off-centre cell, the reverse: a light blue inner disc with minus signs inside a pink ring with plus signs. No labels. The point: light on the plus region raises the cell's firing and light on the minus region lowers it, so uniform light over both does almost nothing.
pub_kuffler_center_surround.png: Kuffler's 1953 recordings as redrawn in Hubel's book Eye, Brain and Vision. Two panels, each a black rectangle with three white stimuli, a small spot, a larger spot and a ring, beside four rows of spike records; a bar under the records marks when the stimulus is on and off. Left panel, an on-centre retinal ganglion cell: the top row is the resting discharge with no stimulus; the small spot on the centre gives a dense burst while the light is on; the larger spot covering centre and surround gives only a few spikes; the ring on the surround silences the cell while on and gives a burst at off. Right panel, an off-centre cell, the mirror image: the small spot silences the cell and gives a burst at off, the large spot does little, the ring gives a burst while on. The point: these cells report local contrast, not brightness.
portrait_hubel_wiesel.png: A black-and-white photograph of David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel in their laboratory, surrounded by racks of recording equipment, oscilloscopes and amplifiers. Hubel, wearing glasses and a dark sweater, sits on the left with one hand on the apparatus; Wiesel, in a patterned sweater, sits on a stool on the right. Both look toward the camera. The portrait sits in the top-right corner of the slide, above the caption Hubel and Wiesel.
pub_hw_mapping.png: Hubel and Wiesel (1962), Text-figure 2: seven receptive fields of cat cells mapped by hand with spots of light, labelled a to g. In the source's legend, crosses mark areas giving excitatory (on) responses and triangles areas giving inhibitory (off) responses; a continuous line through each elongated field marks its axis. Panels a and b, stacked at the left, are circular: a has crosses in the centre inside a ring of triangles, on-centre; b the reverse, off-centre. Panels c to g are elongated along an oblique axis: c has a narrow stripe of crosses between flanks of triangles; d, e and f have a stripe of triangles between flanks of crosses; g has crosses on one side of the axis and triangles on the other, an edge. The point: cortical receptive fields are parallel excitatory and inhibitory strips at one orientation, not concentric rings.
rf_icons_hw_maps.svg: Schematic redrawing of the seven hand maps a to g with pink plus regions and light blue minus regions. Panels a and b at the left are circles: a, a pink plus centre inside a blue minus ring, on-centre; b, a blue minus centre inside a pink plus ring, off-centre. Panels c, d, e and f are ellipses tilted about 48 degrees, each with a pink plus stripe along the long axis between two blue minus flanks. Panel g is an ellipse split along its long axis, blue minus on the upper-left half and pink plus on the lower-right half, an edge. The point: each oriented cell sums light with positive weights along a stripe and negative weights beside it.
pub_hw_ganglion_simple_complex.png: Three columns of black-and-white icons summarizing Hubel and Wiesel's V1. Left column, retinal ganglion or LGN cells: a black disc with a white spot in the centre, an on-centre cell, above a white disc with a black spot, an off-centre cell. Middle column, simple cells: a black disc with a white oblique bar, above a white disc with a black oblique bar, each oriented and at one position. Right column, a complex cell: one large circle with a black oblique bar in the middle and a double-headed arrow across it, showing the bar can sit anywhere in the field at that orientation. The point: a weighted sum builds selectivity for orientation, and a pooling builds tolerance to position.
hw_wiring_frame0.svg: Computed on four model cells; the frame is labelled bar along the row. Top: a grey screen with four on-centre LGN receptive fields in a diagonal row from lower left to upper right, each a circle with a magenta plus centre and blue minus signs on its surround, and a pale yellow bar of light lying along the row through all four centres. Thin lines run from each field to one of four small LGN cell bodies in a row below the screen, each with a spike train to its right, and thick lines from all four converge on a larger cortical simple cell at the bottom with its own spike train. Every LGN cell shows ten spikes and the simple cell shows ten. The point: a bar along the row lights every centre, and the simple cell, which needs most of its inputs active, fires hard.
hw_wiring_frame1.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar rotated 15 degrees away from the row about its middle; the frame is labelled 15 degrees. The bar still crosses the two middle centres but only clips the two end centres. Spike trains: the two end LGN cells show three spikes each, the two middle cells nine each, and the simple cell one spike. The point: a small tilt costs the end cells most of their light, the sum falls below what the simple cell needs, and it nearly stops.
hw_wiring_frame2.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar rotated 30 degrees away from the row; the frame is labelled 30 degrees. The bar crosses only the two middle centres and misses the end cells entirely. Spike trains: the end LGN cells show no spikes, the middle cells six each, and the simple cell none. The point: with only two of four inputs active the simple cell is silent, so its orientation tuning is much narrower than that of its inputs.
hw_wiring_frame3.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar rotated 60 degrees away from the row, now nearly upright; the frame is labelled 60 degrees. The bar passes between the two middle fields and barely touches one centre at a time. Spike trains: the end LGN cells show no spikes, the middle cells one spike each, and the simple cell none.
hw_wiring_frame4.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar rotated 90 degrees, perpendicular to the row; the frame is labelled 90 degrees. The bar crosses the row between the two middle fields and lights no centre. Spike trains: all four LGN cells and the simple cell show no spikes. The point: at the wrong orientation nothing fires.
hw_wiring_frame5.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar back at the row's orientation but shifted sideways by 0.5 units, so it lies along the upper-left edge of the fields, on their inhibitory surrounds and off the plus centres; the frame is labelled right orientation, shifted onto the surrounds. Spike trains: all four LGN cells and the simple cell show no spikes. The point: the right orientation is not enough; the bar must also be in the right place.
hw_wiring_frame6.svg: The same four model LGN cells converging on a cortical simple cell, with the bar at the row's orientation but shifted sideways by 0.8 units, now almost clear of the fields along their upper-left edge; the frame is labelled right orientation, shifted onto the surrounds. Spike trains: all four LGN cells and the simple cell show no spikes. The point: a simple cell is selective for position as well as orientation, because the bar must line up with the plus centres.
pooling_frame0.svg: Computed on model cells. Left panel, Simple cells to complex cell: five overlapping circular receptive fields in a row, numbered 1 to 5, each with a narrow pink ON stripe tilted 30 degrees between wide blue OFF flanks and a spike train above its number; arrows from all five converge on a circle marked sigma, labelled sum, complex cell, with its own spike train. A yellow bar at the same tilt sits at the left edge, just inside field 1. Spike trains: cell 1 three spikes, the others none, the complex cell three. Right panel, Position tuning: response (vertical, 0 to about 1.2) against position of the bar (horizontal, minus 2 to 2); five grey bell-shaped curves numbered 1 to 5 peak at 1.0 at positions minus 1.2, minus 0.6, 0, 0.6 and 1.2; the dark complex-cell curve is drawn only up to the current position, minus 1.600, where it is just rising from zero.
pooling_frame1.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar between fields 1 and 2 at position minus 0.900. Spike trains: cells 1 and 2 five spikes each, cells 3 to 5 none, the complex cell ten. Right panel: the dark complex-cell curve is drawn up to minus 0.9, having risen to a first peak of about 1.1 over cell 1's preferred position and dipped slightly to about 0.98 between cells 1 and 2, where a dot marks the current bar position. The point: two simple cells each half-driven still add up to a full response in the complex cell.
pooling_frame2.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar between fields 2 and 3 at position minus 0.300. Spike trains: cells 2 and 3 five spikes each, the others none, the complex cell ten. Right panel: the dark curve now runs from minus 2 to minus 0.3, with peaks of about 1.1 over the preferred positions of cells 1 and 2 and dips to about 0.98 between them. The point: as the bar moves, different simple cells take over and the complex cell keeps firing.
pooling_frame3.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar centred on field 3 at position 0.000. Spike trains: cell 3 about ten spikes, cells 2 and 4 one each, cells 1 and 5 none, the complex cell about ten. Right panel: the dark curve runs from minus 2 to 0, with three peaks of about 1.1 over cells 1, 2 and 3 and dips to about 0.98 between them; a dot marks the current position at cell 3's peak. The point: a simple cell fires most when the bar is centred on its field.
pooling_frame4.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar between fields 3 and 4 at position 0.300. Spike trains: cells 3 and 4 five spikes each, the others none, the complex cell ten. Right panel: the dark curve runs from minus 2 to 0.3, with peaks of about 1.1 over cells 1, 2 and 3 and dips to about 0.98 between them, the dot sitting in the dip between cells 3 and 4.
pooling_frame5.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar between fields 4 and 5 at position 0.900. Spike trains: cells 4 and 5 five spikes each, the others none, the complex cell ten. Right panel: the dark curve runs from minus 2 to 0.9 with four peaks of about 1.1 over cells 1 to 4 and dips to about 0.98 between them, the dot sitting between cells 4 and 5. The point: the complex cell has fired at every position so far while each simple cell fired only near its own.
pooling_frame6.svg: The same five model simple cells converging on a complex cell, with the bar past the right edge of field 5 at position 1.600. Spike trains: cell 5 three spikes, the others none, the complex cell three. Right panel: the dark complex-cell curve is now drawn over the whole range from minus 2 to 2: it rises from zero near minus 1.6, stays between about 0.98 and 1.1 across the five preferred positions with small dips between them, and falls back to zero past 1.6, while each grey simple-cell curve covers only a narrow range of positions. The point: each simple cell covers a narrow range of positions and the complex cell, their sum, a broad one, at the same orientation.
